previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Factor V Leiden deficiency, chronic anticoagulation with Lovenox, prior pulmonary embolism, and aortic arch thrombus was admitted for recurrent atypical chest pain. The pain was mid-sternal, dull, and pressure-like, unchanged from prior admissions. Evaluation showed normal cardiac enzymes, a benign EKG, and a clear chest X-ray with no acute findings. Given recent imaging and stable vital signs, no additional CT was performed. The pain was attributed to musculoskeletal causes, and the patient was managed without additional narcotics per his contract. He was advised to restart tizanidine, use over-the-counter NSAIDs, and continue all home medications, especially Lovenox. The patient declined psychiatric follow-up despite ongoing chronic pain and anxiety. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with his primary care provider.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to hospital with recurrent flares in your 
longstanding abdominal pain, chest pain and persistent coughing 
of blood for 4 months.  

Because you were not having nausea or vomiting, constipation or 
blood in the stool (a stool blood test was also negative), it 
was unlikely that a small bowel obstruction or impaired blood 
flow to the gut was causing your pain. Your extensive history of 
abdominal surgery, including the procedures involving the 
removal of your spleen, multiple incisional hernia repairs, and 
take-down of surgical scar tissue (aka adhesions), puts you at 
risk for persistent pain from the adhesions.  Also, portions of 
your gut may herniate through scars in the abdominal wall.  An 
abdominal ultrasound was performed, which confirmed the presence 
of abdominal adhesions and a gut herniation through scar tissue 
of the right lower abdominal wall.  Both your adhesions and an 
abdominal hernia are the likely sources of your chronic pain and 
the most recent flare during this hospital presentation.  

You were given iv dilaudid and oral oxycodone for pain control, 
which gave you immediate relief and you were discharged on a 
regimen of oral oxycodone for long term pain control.  You were 
also instructed to follow up with your primary care doctor to 
explore long term options for pain control.
  
For your chest pain, you had an electrocardiogram and three sets 
of cardiac enzymes to rule out the possibility of a heart 
attack.  These tests were normal, and you were continued on your 
home regimen of aspirin, simvastatin and blood pressure 
medications to reduce your risk of heart attack. 

For your coughing up of blood, a weight check revealed that your 
weight adjusted dose of Lovenox needed to be lower than that 
which you were taking at home.  Excessive Lovenox for your body 
weight was likely causing small bleeds in your lungs, 
contributing to the coughing of blood up, as well as causing 
irritation of the lung tissue and contributing to your chest 
pain.  In addition, your tracheobronchomalacia, which is 
fragile, friable tissue likely caused by your long-term smoking, 
may have also bled from trauma of coughing.  A urine analysis 
revealed that you had blood in your urine, further evidence for 
excessive bleeding from your prior Lovenox dose.

To decrease your bleeding, your Lovenox dose was decreased from 
120 mg bid to ___ mg bid.  Additionallly, a lab test was checked 
to make sure that your dose of Lovenox was not causing your 
blood to be thinner than the therapeutic level.  The Factor Xa 
level, which reflects how high your Lovenox dose is, was within 
therapeutic limits but at the upper bound.   

Please monitor your weight regularly (2x/month) and report to 
your primary care physician for significant weight loss or gain 
for the adjustment of your Lovenox dose.  

Please note that the following medications were changed during 
your hospital stay:

1) CHANGE Lovenox ___ mg twice a day to 100 mg twice a day.
2) STOP Percocet and START oxycodone 15 mg every 6 hours as 
needed.
3) CONTINUE Aspirin 81mg daily

All other medications, should be continued as before.

PA AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  The left costophrenic angle is beyond the
field-of-view on the PA image.  Cardiac, mediastinal and hilar contours are
normal.  The lungs are clear.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  No acute intrathoracic abnormality.

HISTORY:  ___ male with hypercoagulable state and chronic abdominal
pain.

COMPARISON:  CT of the torso, ___ and renal ultrasound, ___.

ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND:  The liver is diffusely echogenic.  No focal hepatic
lesions are identified.  There is no intra- or extra-hepatic biliary ductal
dilation.  The common duct measures 3 mm.  The gallbladder is normal, without
evidence of stones.  There is no free fluid in the right upper quadrant.  The
patient is status post splenectomy.  The pancreas is not well seen.

Imaging of the right lower quadrant was performed at the patient's site of
tenderness, which corresponds to a small scar.  At this site, approximately
1.6-cm deep to the skin surface, a hypoechoic ill-defined abnormality
protrudes into the abdominal wall musculature through a 1cm defect into the
abdominal wall and corresponds with the fat-containing anterolateral abdominal
wall hernia identified on CT.  This does not significantly move with Valsalva.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Echogenic liver consistent with fatty infiltration.  Other forms of liver
disease including more significant hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis cannot be
excluded on this study.
